An indicator is something that shows, points to, or signals the state, condition, or existence of something else — usually something you cannot see directly or measure easily on its own.

Think of it this way: you cannot see "danger" itself, but a red warning light on your car's dashboard indicates danger. You cannot see "rain coming" directly, but dark clouds indicate it. The indicator is not the thing itself — it is the visible or measurable sign of that thing.

The word comes from the idea of pointing toward something. An indicator points your attention toward a truth or a condition.
The Most Important Thing to Understand

An indicator is always a stand-in. It represents something bigger, deeper, or less visible.

For example, a thermometer reading is an indicator of your health — the number itself is not your health, but it points to your health condition. A fever of 102°F does not mean anything on its own; what it indicates is that your body is fighting something.

This is the heart of what the word means: you observe the indicator so you can understand something you cannot observe directly.
Where You Will Encounter This Word

The word "indicator" is used across nearly every field. Here is how it functions in each:

In everyday life:
When someone frowns while you are speaking, that frown is an indicator of their disapproval or discomfort. When traffic ahead slows down suddenly, that is an indicator of an obstruction or accident. These are informal, real-life indicators — signs you read to understand a situation.

In vehicles:
In British and Indian English especially, the flashing turn signal on a car or motorcycle is called an indicator. When a driver is about to turn left, they switch on the left indicator — the blinking light that signals (or indicates) their intention to turn. Many people in India use this meaning every single day: "He didn't put the indicator before turning."

In science:
Scientists use indicators to detect things that cannot be seen directly. A classic example is litmus paper, a chemical indicator. If you dip it in a liquid, it turns red or blue — not because the colour matters, but because that colour indicates whether the liquid is acidic or basic. The paper does not tell you the full chemistry; it gives you a readable sign of an underlying condition.

In medicine:
A doctor may say that a high white blood cell count is an indicator of infection. The number on the blood test is not the infection itself — it is a signal that points toward one. Symptoms like shortness of breath may be indicators of heart problems. Medical professionals rely heavily on indicators because the actual disease or condition often cannot be seen without them.

In economics and business:
Economists track economic indicators — statistics and figures that show how a country's economy is performing. GDP growth, unemployment rate, inflation, and consumer spending are all indicators. None of them is "the economy" itself, but together they paint a picture of it.

Businesses use Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) — specific measurable values that indicate whether the business is achieving its goals. For example, a company might track "number of new customers per month" as an indicator of growth.

In dashboards and instruments:
Any gauge, dial, meter, or warning light on a machine is called an indicator. A fuel gauge is a fuel-level indicator. A speedometer is a speed indicator. A warning light that shows your engine is overheating is an indicator. These are all instruments designed specifically to indicate something to you so you can act on it.

In data and research:
When researchers study complex things like poverty, education quality, or happiness, they create indicators — measurable variables that stand in for the larger, harder-to-measure concept. For instance, "school attendance rate" might be used as an indicator of educational engagement. It is not the full picture, but it points toward it.

This is an important nuance. An indicator points to something, but it does not guarantee that thing.

A single indicator can be misleading. For example, one good month of sales is an indicator of business health, but it does not prove the business is doing well overall. Dark clouds indicate rain, but it does not always rain. A symptom can indicate multiple possible diseases.

This is why people often say you should not rely on a single indicator. The more indicators you gather that all point in the same direction, the more confident you can be about what they are indicating.
The Relationship: Indicator and What It Indicates

There is always a two-part relationship:

  • The indicator — the visible, measurable sign
  • What it indicates — the underlying reality or condition

The indicator is chosen because it reliably points to the underlying thing. A good indicator is one where, when the indicator is present or changes, the underlying condition is also reliably present or changed.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see the word "indicator," ask yourself:

"What is this pointing toward? What is it a sign of?"

The indicator is the arrow. It is never the destination — it is what shows you the direction.

An indicator is anything — a sign, signal, measurement, light, statistic, symptom, or substance — that shows, points to, or reveals the state or condition of something else, usually something that is not directly visible or easily understood on its own. It acts as a reliable stand-in that allows you to understand or monitor a deeper reality. The word is used in everyday conversation, medicine, science, economics, vehicles, engineering, and virtually every other domain of life.
